passage:
The common law of defamation has long distinguished between two categories of false statement: those that damage reputation on their face, and those whose injurious effect depends on extrinsic circumstances known to the audience. Courts have traditionally treated the former—called defamation per se—as actionable without proof of actual harm, on the theory that some reputational injuries are so foreseeable that the law may presume damages. Statements accusing a person of criminal conduct, loathsome disease, or serious professional misconduct fall squarely within this category.

Yet this categorical approach has drawn persistent criticism from legal scholars who argue that presumed damages, untethered from any showing of actual loss, permit recoveries wildly disproportionate to genuine injury. The concern intensifies in cases involving media defendants, where the potential chilling effect on constitutionally protected speech is most acute. Since the Supreme Court's decision in Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc., courts have been required, at least in cases involving public figures, to align the availability of presumed damages with some showing of the defendant's fault. Scholars sympathetic to this development argue that it shifts defamation law toward the compensation principle that governs most of tort law: plaintiffs should recover for the harm they actually suffer, not for harm the law imagines they must have suffered.
comparativeBPassage:
A popular view in contemporary tort scholarship holds that defamation law has been successfully rationalized by the constitutional overlay imposed in Gertz and its progeny. On this account, requiring fault and actual-injury proof before presumed damages may be awarded has brought defamation doctrine into alignment with the corrective-justice foundations of the law of torts generally.

This view is too sanguine. The actual-injury requirement, as courts have construed it, encompasses not only pecuniary loss but also emotional distress and reputational harm in the community—harms that are nearly as difficult to falsify as the old presumed-damage rule itself. Plaintiffs' lawyers have learned to dress psychological suffering in the language of 'actual injury,' effectively resurrecting presumed damages under a different label. Moreover, the Gertz framework applies only where the defendant is a media entity or the matter is one of public concern; a substantial body of purely private defamation claims remains governed by the old per se rules. The result is a patchwork: constitutionally sensitive cases receive one treatment, while the majority of defamation suits proceed under doctrinal assumptions that predate the First Amendment's application to state tort law. Far from a rationalized system, modern defamation law is an uneasy coexistence of two incompatible regimes.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following questions is central to both passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Should the Supreme Court's decision in Gertz v. Robert Welch, Inc. be overruled?

choices.label: B
choices.text: How adequately does current defamation law connect damage awards to plaintiffs' actual losses?

choices.label: C
choices.text: What constitutional limits apply to state defamation actions brought by private figures?

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether emotional distress claims should be categorized as defamation per se?

choices.label: E
choices.text: What role do media defendants play in shaping the development of defamation doctrine?

explanations.correct: Passage A argues that defamation per se permits recoveries disproportionate to actual loss and discusses the move toward a compensation principle; passage B questions whether the Gertz reforms genuinely achieved injury-based recovery. Both passages are organized around whether damage awards reflect real harm.
explanations.A: Neither passage calls for Gertz to be overruled; passage B criticizes its limited scope, not its existence.
explanations.B: Correct. Both passages center on whether defamation recoveries are properly tied to demonstrated harm.
explanations.C: Only passage A briefly touches on public figures; neither passage focuses on private figures' constitutional limits.
explanations.D: Emotional distress is raised only in passage B and only as an example, not the central question.
explanations.E: Passage A mentions media defendants, but passage B does not focus on their role; neither treats this as the central issue.

questions.questionStem: The authors of the two passages would be most likely to disagree over which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Whether defamation per se traditionally permitted recovery without proof of actual loss

choices.label: B
choices.text: Whether Gertz imposed any requirement of fault on media defendants

choices.label: C
choices.text: Whether the post-Gertz defamation framework has successfully rationalized damages doctrine

choices.label: D
choices.text: Whether statements accusing someone of criminal conduct can damage reputation

choices.label: E
choices.text: Whether a chilling effect on speech is a legitimate concern in defamation cases

explanations.correct: Passage A presents the Gertz development approvingly—scholars 'sympathetic to this development' see it as moving toward the compensation principle. Passage B opens by targeting exactly this approving view as 'too sanguine,' arguing the reforms failed. The rationalization of the doctrine is the direct point of contention.
explanations.A: Both passages accept this as the traditional rule; no disagreement exists.
explanations.B: Neither passage disputes Gertz's fault requirement; passage B questions only its scope.
explanations.C: Correct. Passage A endorses the Gertz reforms; passage B argues they are insufficient.
explanations.D: Both passages treat this as settled background; neither contests it.
explanations.E: Passage A raises the chilling-effect concern approvingly; passage B does not dispute the concern itself.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following is mentioned in passage B but not in passage A as a problem with current defamation law?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Damage awards may be disproportionate to the reputational harm plaintiffs actually suffer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Presumed damages create a chilling effect on constitutionally protected speech.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Private defamation claims largely remain governed by pre-Gertz per se rules.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The categorical approach of defamation per se has been criticized by legal scholars.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Courts have required some showing of fault in cases involving public figures.

explanations.correct: Passage B specifically identifies that a 'substantial body of purely private defamation claims remains governed by the old per se rules,' creating a patchwork system. Passage A does not address the continued application of per se rules to private claims.
explanations.A: Passage A explicitly raises disproportionate recoveries as a criticism; it is not unique to passage B.
explanations.B: The chilling-effect concern appears in passage A, not uniquely in passage B.
explanations.C: Correct. Only passage B identifies the private-claim carve-out as a structural defect.
explanations.D: Passage A introduces this criticism; it is not unique to passage B.
explanations.E: Both passages reference the fault requirement from Gertz; it is not unique to either.

questions.questionStem: It can be inferred from passage B that the author would most likely agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The Gertz decision should be extended to all defamation suits, including those involving purely private matters.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Requiring proof of fault is sufficient by itself to bring defamation law into line with corrective-justice principles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Courts have interpreted 'actual injury' so broadly that the requirement offers little meaningful constraint on damage awards.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Emotional distress damages should be categorically excluded from defamation recoveries.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The constitutional overlay imposed by Gertz was an improper exercise of Supreme Court authority.

explanations.correct: Passage B argues that courts have construed 'actual injury' to include emotional distress and reputational harm 'nearly as difficult to falsify as the old presumed-damage rule,' effectively resurrecting presumed damages under a new label. The inference that the actual-injury requirement is not a meaningful constraint follows directly.
explanations.A: Passage B notes the private-defamation gap but does not explicitly advocate for extending Gertz to all suits; that goes beyond what the text supports.
explanations.B: Passage B argues the reforms are insufficient even with the fault requirement; this choice contradicts the passage's thesis.
explanations.C: Correct. This is supported by passage B's claim that 'actual injury' is nearly as unfalsifiable as the old presumed-damage rule.
explanations.D: Passage B criticizes the use of emotional distress claims but does not advocate categorically excluding them.
explanations.E: Passage B critiques the limited scope of Gertz but does not question the Court's authority to decide it.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage A most likely mentions the 'compensation principle' (last sentence) in order to

choices.label: A
choices.text: introduce a new theory of tort recovery that has not previously been applied to defamation cases

choices.label: B
choices.text: characterize the underlying rationale that critics of presumed damages invoke to support the post-Gertz trend

choices.label: C
choices.text: argue that defamation law should be abolished in favor of a general tort of unjust enrichment

choices.label: D
choices.text: distinguish the compensation principle from the corrective-justice principle discussed by scholars

choices.label: E
choices.text: concede that the compensation principle is inadequate to resolve the chilling-effect problem

explanations.correct: The final sentence of passage A describes the view of 'scholars sympathetic to this development,' explaining that requiring fault and actual-injury proof aligns defamation law with 'the compensation principle that governs most of tort law.' The author is characterizing the normative foundation of the reform position, not endorsing or attacking it independently.
explanations.A: The compensation principle is presented as an established feature of most tort law, not a novel theory.
explanations.B: Correct. The author uses the compensation principle to explain the theoretical basis for the Gertz-era reforms as seen by their supporters.
explanations.C: No such argument appears anywhere in passage A.
explanations.D: Passage A does not distinguish between compensation and corrective justice; passage B uses the term 'corrective justice.'
explanations.E: Passage A does not concede any inadequacy of the compensation principle; it presents the principle neutrally as the reformers' rationale.

questions.questionStem: Which one of the following most accurately describes the relationship between the two passages?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Passage A presents a historical overview of defamation doctrine, and passage B applies that overview to a specific recent case.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Passage A describes a reform trend and the scholarly arguments supporting it, and passage B argues that those arguments overstate the success of the reform.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Passage A endorses the per se rules in defamation, and passage B offers a rebuttal on behalf of the Gertz framework.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Passage A identifies a problem with defamation law, and passage B proposes a legislative solution to that problem.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Passage A and passage B both criticize the Gertz decision from different constitutional perspectives.

explanations.correct: Passage A traces the traditional per se doctrine, identifies its scholarly critics, and describes the Gertz reforms sympathetically as moving toward the compensation principle. Passage B targets the view that this reform succeeded as 'too sanguine' and catalogs the ways it fell short. This is a point/counterpoint structure where B challenges the position A presents.
explanations.A: Passage A is not purely historical, and passage B does not apply anything to a specific case.
explanations.B: Correct. Passage A builds the case for reform; passage B disputes that the reform achieved its goals.
explanations.C: Passage A criticizes the per se rules, not endorses them; the relationship is reversed.
explanations.D: Passage B offers no legislative proposal; it is a scholarly critique.
explanations.E: Neither passage criticizes Gertz on constitutional grounds; passage B questions its practical scope.

questions.questionStem: The author of passage B would be most likely to make which one of the following criticisms about the claim in passage A that the post-Gertz trend moves defamation law toward 'the compensation principle'?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The claim ignores the fact that Gertz introduced a fault requirement that most scholars consider too lenient toward media defendants.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The claim is accurate as a description of the constitutional cases but overstates the reform's reach, since private defamation claims continue to operate under the per se presumed-damage rules.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The claim incorrectly attributes the compensation principle to tort law generally, when in fact it originated in contract law.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The claim relies on a misreading of Gertz, which was concerned with fault, not with limiting the availability of damages.

choices.label: E
choices.text: The claim exaggerates the degree to which scholars have endorsed the post-Gertz framework.

explanations.correct: Passage B's core criticism is that the Gertz reforms apply only where a media defendant or public-concern matter is involved, leaving 'a substantial body of purely private defamation claims' under the old per se rules. This is exactly the objection that the compensation-principle claim overstates the reform's scope.
explanations.A: Passage B does not discuss the leniency of the fault standard toward media defendants.
explanations.B: Correct. Passage B identifies the private-claim carve-out as the reason the reform falls short of the compensation principle's reach.
explanations.C: Passage B does not dispute the intellectual origin of the compensation principle.
explanations.D: Passage B does not claim that Gertz was unconcerned with damages; in fact, it discusses the actual-injury requirement Gertz introduced.
explanations.E: Passage B targets the view of scholars who find the reforms successful, but does not dispute that scholars have endorsed the framework.
